subject: Nominal model giving strange results after update

messages.author: 7f8c7a483a14100b
messages.subject: Nominal model giving strange results after update
parts:
Greetings,

I used mirt a couple months ago to analyze a set of nominal data. Each item has between 5 and 9 possible responses (one of which is considered correct), and mirt handled it beautifully. I tried to rerun the analysis today, and it's giving results that don't match those from before. Here's what I've found: using a machine with mirt 1.24 and R 3.4.1 gives the same results as before, but using a machine with mirt 1.26 and R 3.4.3 gives the strange results. As an example of the strangeness I've included an example itemplot that is consistent with what I found before. (I'm sorry that I do not have the comparison plot to attach.) In this plot option H has a small peak around theta = 0.75. In the analyses using mirt 1.26 this peak does not exist, and option D (which is flat and nearly invisible in the attached plot) sharply increases near theta = -2; this is accompanied by a sharp decrease in option A for low theta.

I also noticed that with mirt 1.24 the mirt function goes through more than a hundred iterations before producing a result, but in mirt 1.26 it only goes through 2 iterations. perhaps this is part of the issue.

Does the updated mirt package assume a different data format than its predecessor? I've searched this forum and some other places, but I've been unable to locate the answer. To run mirt 1.24 I formatted the data so that responses are numeric, and the correct response for each question has value 9 (with all other responses being integers less than 9).

Thank you very much for any help.

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: Nominal model giving strange results after update
parts:
It's possible that some settings have changed across major version iterations, but I think the issue here may have been of over-interpretation of the initial solution. The nominal response model is extremely flexible, and as such tends to have rather high-sampling variability of the estimates. What that means is that, depending on when the model terminates in the estimation, the point estimates may be very different near the ML location, and yet give similar log-likelihood values. Hence, the shape of the curves, when considering this sampling variability, may differ wildly simply due to the likelihood of the parameter range.  

With 9 nominal response categories, the SEs would be rather large, and so the certainty of where the true parameter values are is largely a mystery (you'd need extremely large sample sizes to reduce the SE of these kinds of models, 10000+ likely). This is why the nominal model is generally "exploratory", since it gives a general idea of what the IRT function should look like, but the exact shape is too difficult for it to capture due to it's over-flexibility and large sampling variability. HTH.  

Phil

messages.author: 7f8c7a483a14100b
messages.subject: Re: Nominal model giving strange results after update
parts:
Thank you very much for your response, Phil. 
After playing around a bit more I think the issue is that the mirt function terminates after only 2 iterations. I know that NCYCLES will increase the maximum possible number of iterations, but is there a way to specify a minimum number? I realize this sounds a little ridiculous because once the model converges there's no reason to keep running. I just find it strange that running the same commands using the same data (over 14,000 samples) would converge with such different results in two different versions of the package. I suppose it's due to the fact that the nominal model is so flexible, as you said. I also wonder if it has something to do with the way in which mirt estimates the theta parameter for nominal data.

After looking more, I was able to use the example in the mirt documentation of the combined nominal/2PL model based on Suh and Bolt (2010). This analysis provided results that are consistent with my original analysis.

Thanks again,
Trevor

On Tue, Jan 30, 2018 at 12:41 PM, Trevor Smith <smi...@rowan.edu> wrote:
Thank you very much for your response, Phil. 
After playing around a bit more I think the issue is that the mirt function terminates after only 2 iterations.

I see, this could be a starting values problem then. It might be good to pass GenRandomPars = TRUE to mirt to start at a new, randomly drawn set of parameters to try and avoid the initial issue. Early termination like that is generally a sign that the M-step optimizer got confused somehow with the model (quickly moved into a region it couldn't break out of).

I know that NCYCLES will increase the maximum possible number of iterations, but is there a way to specify a minimum number? I realize this sounds a little ridiculous because once the model converges there's no reason to keep running. I just find it strange that running the same commands using the same data (over 14,000 samples) would converge with such different results in two different versions of the package. I suppose it's due to the fact that the nominal model is so flexible, as you said. I also wonder if it has something to do with the way in which mirt estimates the theta parameter for nominal data.
theta is never estimated, it is integrated out of the likelihood functions.

After looking more, I was able to use the example in the mirt documentation of the combined nominal/2PL model based on Suh and Bolt (2010). This analysis provided results that are consistent with my original analysis.

Yes, I would agree the nested-logit model is much more robust because it has a directional component built in. 

Phil

Thanks again,
Trevor
